title: Listening to the Sky: Radio Astronomy
objective: After this level you can explain what radio telescopes detect and why they are so large.
summary: Radio telescopes catch long radio waves that pierce dust and work day or night. Linked dishes act like one giant telescope.

cards.headline: Some telescopes don’t need darkness. They work at noon, through clouds.
cards.body: They're tuned to a kind of light that clouds and daylight can't stop. Meet the telescopes that listen instead of look.

cards.headline: A new window
cards.body: In the early 1930s, Karl Jansky picked up radio waves coming from the Milky Way. Radio astronomy was born. Radio waves pass through cosmic dust and Earth's clouds, and radio telescopes can observe in daylight. A cloudy afternoon? A radio astronomer barely notices. Suddenly the sky could be studied around the clock.

cards.headline: Why the dishes are huge
cards.body: Remember the light bucket from Level 33? Radio waves are very long, so seeing fine detail takes an enormous dish. And when one dish isn't enough, astronomers link many dishes into an array that works together like one much larger telescope. Can't build a bigger bucket? Build a team of buckets.

cards.fact: The Very Large Array in New Mexico links 27 radio dishes.
cards.context: Spread out over up to 36 km, they work together like a single dish of that size. Twenty-seven dishes, one enormous eye on the radio sky. The name isn't modest, but it is accurate.

questions.prompt: What did Karl Jansky detect in the early 1930s?

options.label: The first planet beyond Neptune
options.rationale: He detected radio waves, not a planet.

options.label: Radio waves coming from the Milky Way

questions.explanation: Jansky’s detection of radio waves from the Milky Way launched radio astronomy.

questions.prompt: Why are radio telescopes usually so much bigger than optical ones?

options.label: Radio sources are much closer than stars
Radio waves are very long, so fine detail needs a huge dish
Radio waves travel more slowly than light
options.rationale: They travel at the speed of light.

options.label: Radio telescopes must block the daylight

questions.explanation: The longer the wavelength, the bigger the dish must be to see fine detail. Radio waves are the longest of all.

questions.prompt: From Level 33: a bigger aperture shows finer detail. How do radio astronomers get an aperture bigger than any single dish?

options.label: By cooling the dishes to very low temperatures
options.rationale: Cooling reduces noise; it doesn’t enlarge the aperture.

options.label: By pointing the dishes at brighter sources
By using lenses instead of dishes
By linking many dishes into one array

questions.explanation: Linked dishes work together like one telescope as large as the spread of the array.
